note.text:
The nitrogen cycle is how nitrogen passes between the air, the soil and living things.
• Fixation: nitrogen from the air is turned into compounds plants can use. By nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium) in the root nodules of legumes such as beans and groundnuts; by lightning, which makes nitrogen oxides that reach the soil in rain; and by industry, in the Haber process.
• Absorption: plant roots take in nitrates and build them into proteins. Animals get their protein by eating plants.
• Decay: bacteria of decay break down dead plants, animals and waste into ammonium compounds.
• Nitrification: nitrifying bacteria change ammonium compounds into nitrites (Nitrosomonas) and then nitrates (Nitrobacter).
• Denitrification: in waterlogged soil, denitrifying bacteria change nitrates back into nitrogen gas, which returns to the air.
Farmers keep the soil rich by rotating crops with legumes and by adding fertilisers.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to name and explain each stage of the nitrogen cycle and say how farming practices affect it.
Builds on: Lesson {11} (nitrogen is unreactive) and Form Three food chains.
Leads to: Lesson {17} (fertilisers) and the study of soil fertility in Biology and Agriculture.

sections.heading: Getting nitrogen into living things
Returning nitrogen to the soil and the air
sections.text:
• DECAY: when plants and animals die, and in their waste, bacteria of decay break the protein down into ammonium compounds.
• NITRIFICATION: nitrifying bacteria change these into nitrites (Nitrosomonas) and then into nitrates (Nitrobacter), which plants can use again.
• DENITRIFICATION: in waterlogged soil, where there is little air, denitrifying bacteria change nitrates back into nitrogen gas, and the soil loses nitrogen to the air.
Farmers work with the cycle: they rotate crops with legumes, plough crop residues back in, drain waterlogged land, and add fertilisers to replace the nitrogen taken away in the harvest.

mistake.wrong: plants take nitrogen straight from the air
mistake.right: they take nitrates from the soil
mistake.why: Only certain bacteria can use nitrogen gas; plants need it already fixed.

worked_example.problem: Explain why planting beans in a field helps the maize grown there the following year.
steps: Beans are legumes, and their roots carry nodules holding nitrogen-fixing bacteria.
These bacteria change nitrogen from the air into compounds the plant can use.
When the bean plants die and decay, that fixed nitrogen is left in the soil as ammonium compounds.
Nitrifying bacteria change these into nitrates, which the maize roots can take in.
worked_example.answer: the bacteria in the bean root nodules leave fixed nitrogen in the soil

cards.idea: Fixation turns nitrogen gas into compounds plants can use.
example: by bacteria in root nodules, by lightning, and in the Haber process

cards.idea: Nitrifying bacteria turn ammonium compounds into nitrites and then nitrates.
example: decay gives ammonium compounds; nitrification gives nitrates

pick.q: Which stage comes immediately after the decay of a dead plant?
pick.r: Nitrification: the ammonium compounds become nitrites and then nitrates
pick.y: Decay gives ammonium compounds, which nitrifying bacteria change into nitrates.

pick.q: A field is waterlogged for several weeks. What is likely to happen to its nitrates?
pick.r: Denitrifying bacteria change them into nitrogen gas, which escapes
pick.w2: They turn into ammonia and stay in the soil
pick.y: Denitrifying bacteria work where there is little air, so waterlogged soil loses nitrogen.

pick.q: How does nitrogen from the air reach the protein of a cow?
pick.r: Fixation to nitrates, absorption by a plant, then the cow eats the plant
pick.w1: The cow breathes in nitrogen and uses it directly
pick.w2: The cow absorbs nitrates through its skin
pick.w3: Lightning puts nitrogen straight into the cow's food
pick.y: Animals cannot use nitrogen gas: it must pass through fixation and then through plants.

cards.idea: Denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen to the air from waterlogged soil.
example: which is why waterlogged fields lose their fertility

pick.r: Changing nitrogen from the air into a compound that plants can use
w: Taking nitrates out of the soil
Changing nitrates back into nitrogen gas
Holding nitrogen in the air so it cannot escape
e: Taking nitrates out of the soil is what plants do when they absorb them.
That is denitrification, the opposite process.
Nitrogen does not need to be held in; the problem is that plants cannot use it as a gas.
pick.y: Plants cannot use nitrogen gas, so it must first be fixed into ammonia or nitrates.

pick.q: Which bacteria live in the root nodules of leguminous plants such as beans and groundnuts?
e: Denitrifying bacteria live in waterlogged soil and give nitrogen back to the air.
Nitrifying bacteria live free in the soil and change ammonium compounds into nitrates.
Bacteria of decay break down dead matter; they do not live in root nodules.
pick.y: Rhizobium in the nodules fixes nitrogen from the air, which is why legumes enrich the soil.

pick.r: They change ammonium compounds into nitrites and then into nitrates
w: They change nitrates into nitrogen gas
They fix nitrogen from the air
They break down protein in dead plants
e: That is nitrogen fixation, done by different bacteria.
That is done by the bacteria of decay, which give ammonium compounds.
pick.y: Nitrosomonas gives nitrites and Nitrobacter gives nitrates, which the plant roots can absorb.

pick.r: Nitrates in the soil are changed back into nitrogen gas
w: Nitrogen gas is changed into nitrates
e: That is decay, carried out by bacteria of decay.
pick.y: Denitrifying bacteria work in waterlogged soil with little air, and the soil loses nitrogen to the atmosphere.

pick.q: How does lightning take part in the nitrogen cycle?
pick.r: Its very high temperature makes nitrogen and oxygen combine, and the oxides dissolve in rain as nitric acid
w: It splits nitrates in the soil
It has no part in the cycle
e: Lightning acts on the air, not on the soil.
Its effect is to add fixed nitrogen, not to remove bacteria.
It is one of the natural ways nitrogen is fixed.
pick.y: {formula('N2')} + {formula('O2')} → {2}{formula('NO')} in the flash; the acid formed reaches the soil as nitrate.

pick.q: Why do farmers often grow beans or groundnuts between crops of maize?
pick.r: The bacteria in their root nodules put fixed nitrogen back into the soil
w: They take nitrates out of the soil faster
They keep insects away from the maize
They use less water than maize
e: Legumes add nitrogen to the soil rather than stripping it.
Keeping insects away is not the reason for this rotation.
Water use is not what makes this rotation useful.
pick.y: Legumes carry nitrogen-fixing bacteria, so the soil is richer in nitrogen for the next crop.

pick.q: Put the stages of the nitrogen cycle in order, starting from nitrogen in the air.
s: Nitrogen in the air is fixed by bacteria or by lightning
Plant roots absorb the nitrates and build proteins
Animals eat the plants, and both die and decay
Denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen gas to the air

pick.q: Put these stages of decay and nitrification in order.
s: A plant dies and falls on the soil
Bacteria of decay break down its protein
Ammonium compounds are left in the soil
Nitrobacter changes the nitrites into nitrates

pick.q: Put the stages by which lightning adds nitrogen to the soil in order.
s: A lightning flash heats the air to a very high temperature
Nitrogen and oxygen combine to give nitrogen oxide
The nitrogen oxide is oxidised to nitrogen dioxide in the air
The nitrogen dioxide dissolves in rain to give an acid
The acid reaches the soil, where it forms nitrates

pick.q: Why does a farmer plough and drain a waterlogged field?
pick.r: To let air into the soil, so that denitrifying bacteria do not take the nitrates away
pick.y: Denitrifying bacteria work where there is little air, so draining the soil protects its nitrates.

pick.q: Why does burning crop residues instead of ploughing them in waste nitrogen?
pick.r: The nitrogen in the plants escapes into the air instead of decaying into the soil
pick.w1: Burning makes the soil too hot for roots
pick.w2: Ash contains no minerals at all
pick.w3: Burning kills the plants, which were still growing
pick.y: Ploughing the residues in lets bacteria of decay return their nitrogen to the soil.

pick.q: A farmer grows maize in the same field every year without fertiliser. What happens to the yield?
pick.r: It falls, because each crop removes nitrates that are not replaced
pick.w1: It rises, because the soil gets used to maize
pick.w2: It stays the same for ever
pick.w3: It falls, because lightning stops fixing nitrogen
pick.y: Harvesting takes the nitrogen away in the grain, so the soil must be replenished.
